name: Amira Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a grader at Mount Selwyn, the iron ore mine up on the plateau. My job is keeping the haul roads smooth, so the big trucks don't wreck their tyres, which cost more than my house. I start at six with a pre-start check, then I'm up and down the same eight kilometres of road all day, cutting the ruts, spreading the gravel, and the water cart comes behind me. It's satisfying when a road is perfect. The tiring part is the concentration, because a 200-tonne truck coming the other way doesn't brake for you.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Viktor and I had a café on Market Street for fifteen years. When the mine had its big downturn a few years back, half the town stopped buying coffee and we went under. We still owe the bank for the coffee machine and the fit-out, so there's not much left over, maybe a couple of weeks of bills in savings. Viktor drives a delivery van now and I came here at fifty-four, which is three, nearly four years ago. I'm still not quick on the grader, but I'm careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI Plateau. That would give me time, which is what I need most. Every month without changes is a month I get better on the grader and the café loan gets smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the crew meeting I'd say good, let's get on with the roads. I'm not one for big speeches. To Viktor I'd say at least we know where we stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI was never the thing I lay awake about. Iron ore prices are, because the last downturn closed our café and half of Market Street with it. If the price drops again, the mine cuts the newest people first, and I'm nearly four years in and still the slowest grader on the plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep paying the café loan, 300 a month, as planned. I'd ask the supervisor for time on the steeper ramps so I get better where it counts. In about a year I'd restart weekend catering, birthday cakes and funeral trays, just a little extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady with it. I've been through one downturn with no plan, and I won't do that again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know a downturn was coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When we had the café, the mine guys stopped buying the second cup of coffee six months before the layoffs. Now I watch the canteen instead. If the overtime dries up, I'll know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a slowdown mean for Viktor's van job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Viktor delivers for the building suppliers, and when the mine slows, nobody builds. So we'd both feel it at once, which is the thing I fear most. One wage we can live on, just. None we can't.

say: Good, let's get on with **the roads**.
To Viktor I'd say at least we know **where we stand**.
think: AI was never what kept me up; **iron ore prices** are, since the last downturn closed our café.
The mine cuts **the newest people** first in a downturn.
I'm nearly four years in and still **the slowest grader** on the plateau.
do: Keeps paying **the café loan** at 300 a month as planned.
Asks for time on **the steeper ramps** to get better where it counts.
Restarts **weekend catering** in about a year for a little extra.
feel: **Anxious but steady**, determined never again to face a downturn with no plan.
S0.quote: When we had the café, the mine guys stopped buying the second cup of coffee six months before the layoffs.
fieldNote: Amira's worry in a plateau is **the iron ore price**, which already cost her a café.
She and Viktor both depend on the mine's fortunes, so a downturn would hit **both wages** at once.
She reads **the canteen's overtime** the way she once read coffee orders.

steps.text: Keep paying 300 a month off the old café loan
Ask for time on the steeper haul road ramps
Restart weekend catering in about a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks first, robots later. My grader's hands-on, so it waits. But the office that plans the haul roads and the people who book Viktor's deliveries are exactly that list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the crew meeting I'd say the robots are slow in this one, so let's ask the company now what its plan is for the graders and get our names on any training. I'd say it calmly. Shouting never changed a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a computer that plans every haul road will also count every pass I make, and it'll notice I'm the slow one. And Viktor's company would use a program to plan the delivery routes, so they'd need four vans instead of five. That's both of us at risk at once, which is the thing I fear most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd restart the weekend catering straight away, with the phone AI doing the orders and the prices, which is the part I'm worst at. I'd put my name down for the automated grader training once the first group reports back. And I'd put any catering money onto the café loan and skip the holiday to my sister's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. I'd sleep badly and then get up and work through my list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the route planning matter so much for Viktor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Viktor's the newest driver at the building suppliers, like I'm the newest grader. If a program makes the routes tighter, they keep four vans and lose the fifth, and the fifth is always the new man. We'd find out on the same Friday, knowing our luck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the computer would count your passes. Does that already happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The new GPS on the grader already shows how long each section took me. He hasn't said anything yet, but my supervisor looks at the grader's tablet before he looks at the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 for the hands. That's the year Viktor's van and my grader go together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the crew meeting I'd say we have three years before the machines can do our work, so let's find out the company's plan now and make our own. I'd say it calmly. I'm not one for shouting, and shouting wouldn't change the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the thinking machines in 2028 don't touch my grader much, maybe the planning of which road to cut. But in 2031 the robots come for the grader and for Viktor's delivery van in the same year, and that's my nightmare, both at once. I'd be sixty-three, with the pension still a couple of years off and maybe still owing the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every spare cent on the café loan, plus about two hundred a month from catering, to clear it before 2031. I'd restart the weekend catering straight away, and use the AI on my phone for the orders and prices, because by 2028 it'll be good at that. And I'd go to the council in the first year to ask what help there is for older workers, before we're desperate, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly, but with a list. I'd sleep badly, but I'd get up and do the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why go to the council before you need help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the café closed, we waited until the bank letters came, and by then every office had a queue. I learned that the hard way. This time I'd want my name on whatever list there is while the queue is short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the catering be enough if both jobs went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not by itself. Birthday cakes and funeral trays won't pay a mortgage on a café that doesn't exist. But a hundred a week from the catering would keep the lights on while we work out the rest.

think: The 2028 machines barely touch my grader, but in 2031 robots take the grader and **Viktor's van** together.

Restarts **weekend catering** at once, with the phone AI on orders and prices.
Goes to **the council** in year one to ask about help for older workers.
feel: **Scared but organised**: she'd sleep badly, then get up and work through her list.
S2.quote: Birthday cakes and funeral trays won't pay a mortgage on a café that doesn't exist.
fieldNote: Amira saw that the three-year gap lands **both their jobs** in the same year, the outcome she fears most.
Her plan is to **clear the café loan** first and get on the council's list early.
The café taught her that **waiting for the letters** costs you.

steps.text: Put every spare cent and catering money on the café loan before 2031
Restart weekend catering now, using the phone AI for orders and prices
Ask the council in year one about help for older workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2034 for the robots. I'd be sixty-six. That's past the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the crew meeting this is the sensible one, there's time to plan properly. Let the company say what it's doing and we'll do the same. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd make it. The robot graders and the robot vans come in 2034, and I'd be retiring around then anyway. If I can clear the café loan in three years, I can face the robots with nothing owing, and that changes everything for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put about two hundred a month of catering money onto the loan for three years. I'd take the automated grader course once the first group reports back, so I'm useful in the last years. After the loan's cleared, I'd start saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. It's a plan I can see the end of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Viktor in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be sixty-five in 2034, so he'd be right at the edge too. It would be close for both of us, but close is better than over. We'd make it if nothing else breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the thinking machines in 2031 change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the catering. The AI would do the ordering and the pricing better than me. I'd let it, and spend my time on the pastries, which is the part people pay for.

Let the company say what it's doing and **we'll do the same**.
think: I'd **make it**, because robot graders and vans come in 2034, around when I'd retire anyway.
If I clear the café loan in three years, I face the robots **with nothing owing**.

Takes **the automated grader course** once the first group reports back.
Starts **saving** once the loan is cleared.
feel: **Uneasy but steady**, with a plan she can see the end of.
S3.quote: If I can clear the café loan in three years, I can face the robots with nothing owing, and that changes everything for me.
fieldNote: With robots due in 2034, she and Viktor reach retirement **right at the edge**.
Her steady approach shows in waiting for **the first group** before taking the course.
She'd let AI take **the business side** of catering and keep the baking.

steps.text: Put about two hundred a month of catering money on the café loan
Keep the weekend catering going, with AI doing orders and pricing
Take the automated grader course once the first group reports back

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years and thirteen. I'd be retired well before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this one's fine for people my age and a warning for the young ones. At the crew meeting I'd tell the young ones to learn the new systems early. I'd say it kindly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means the robots arrive at my retirement party, not my job interview. My worry would be the town after we're gone. If the mine runs itself, who buys coffee?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd clear the café loan in the first three years, then save for retirement. I'd learn the new grader systems alongside the others when they come. And I'd keep the catering going for money and for something to do after I stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the first picture where the timing works for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would retirement look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pastries on Saturdays, Viktor fixing the neighbours' cars, grandchildren on Sundays. Small things, but ours. Nothing owed to anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'who buys coffee'. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the mine had a bad year, nobody bought coffee, and our café died. A mine that runs itself doesn't stop for a flat white. That's the town's worry, not mine, but I'd still feel it.

The young ones should **learn the new systems** early.
think: Ten years means robots arrive at **my retirement party**, not my job interview.
My worry would be **the town**: if the mine runs itself, who buys coffee?

S4.quote: Ten years means the robots arrive at my retirement party, not my job interview.
fieldNote: With the long timeline Amira expects to retire first and is **calm** for the first time in the AGI pictures.
Her concern turns to **the town's economy**, shaped by watching her café die in a downturn.
Her plan is the same steady **debt-then-savings** path.

steps.text: Clear the café loan in three years, then save for retirement
Keep the weekend catering going into retirement
Keep grading roads at Mount Selwyn and learn new systems with the crew

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the robots would take Viktor's van and my grader in the same year, before my pension, and we might still owe the bank. What would help is the government letting people over fifty-five freeze business debts if they lose their jobs to automation, and a bit of help to start something small, like my catering. Practical help, not speeches.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. When the mine had a bad year, my café died. If the mine goes, every café, every hairdresser, every school goes with it. People forget that.

headlineQuote: When the mine had a bad year, my café died. If the mine goes, every café, every hairdresser, every school goes with it.
portrait: Amira Ziegler, 58, grades **the haul roads** at the Mount Selwyn iron ore mine, after her café failed in a mining downturn.
She and Viktor, now a van driver, still **owe the bank** for the café and have about two weeks of savings.
In a plateau she's **anxious** about the iron ore price, which could cut both their jobs at once.
Steady change keeps her **anxious**, as AI route planning and grader tracking expose two newest workers.
AGI by 2028 **alarms** her; with five or ten years she has a debt-then-savings plan with real numbers.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would take her grader and Viktor's van in the same year, before her pension.
They might **still owe** the bank then.
whatWouldHelp: Letting older workers who lose jobs to automation **freeze business debts**.
Help to start **something small**, like her catering.
